The Settlement and the Dictators

Versailles, the Mandates, and Lenin's Russia

Mini-lesson · Mr. Magister

Making the Peace

1January 1919: the conference in Paris
2June 28, 1919: the treaty at Versailles
3A new map for Europe and the Middle East
4The League of Nations without America
5Lenin's Russia: soviets, Cheka, and civil war
Today's Focus

Why did a peace meant to end the war please almost no one, and how did a radical party seize Russia while the world was looking elsewhere?

After the armistice came the harder task of making peace. Today you will see how the victors redrew the map, why the settlement pleased almost no one, and how a radical party seized Russia while the world was looking elsewhere.

Objectives
  1. Describe the main terms of the Treaty of Versailles and the new map of Europe and the Middle East.
  2. Explain why the League of Nations lacked the strength to enforce the peace.
  3. Explain how Lenin and the Bolsheviks won power and built a one-party state in Russia.
Quick Check-in

In 1919 the victors met in Paris to make peace with Germany. Before you read: what do you expect the treaty did?

Words

Subject vocabulary
armisticeAR-mih-stisAn agreement by both sides in a war to stop fighting, usually before a final peace treaty is made.
mandateMAN-daytAfter World War I, a territory taken from a defeated power and governed by another nation under the League of Nations, until it was ready to govern itself.
reparationsrep-uh-RAY-shunzPayments that a defeated nation is required to make to the winners for the damage caused by a war.
self-determinationself-dih-TER-mih-NAY-shunThe principle that each people has the right to choose its own government and its own nation.
Foreign language vocabulary
sovietSOH-vee-etA Russian word meaning "council." In 1917 it named the councils of workers and soldiers that arose across Russia, and later it named the whole Soviet state.
BolshevikBOHL-shuh-vikFrom the Russian word for "majority." It names the radical party led by Vladimir Lenin that took power in Russia in 1917.

Versailles, the Mandates, and Lenin's Russia

Part 1

Paris, 1919

Chapter 1Paris, 1919
Chapter 1

Paris, 1919

In January 1919 delegates from some thirty countries gathered in Paris. Germany and Russia were not invited. The real decisions were made by four men: President Woodrow Wilson of the United States, Prime Minister David Lloyd George of Britain, Prime Minister Georges Clemenceau of France, and Vittorio Orlando of Italy, who walked out when Italy did not receive the lands it had been promised.

The setting was strange. Wilson had crossed the Atlantic in December, the first American president to travel to Europe while in office, and was cheered by crowds in Paris and London. Clemenceau, the oldest of the four and nicknamed the Tiger, was shot and wounded by a gunman in February but returned to the talks within days. Germany had asked for the armistice in the hope of a peace based on Wilson's points, and while the leaders argued, the British blockade of Germany continued, so that hunger went on in German towns until July. Beyond the doors of the conference, new governments, peoples, and borders were waiting for a decision.

Each came with different aims. Wilson had laid out his hopes in the Fourteen Points of January 1918, which you will read. They called for open diplomacy, freedom of the seas, lower trade barriers, smaller armies, and the self-determination of peoples. The last point proposed a League of Nations, to keep peace by collective action. Clemenceau, whose country had lost over a million men and had been invaded twice in fifty years, wanted security above all. Lloyd George had just won an election in which crowds shouted that Germany must pay, yet he also feared pushing Germany too hard.

Part 2

The Treaty of Versailles

Chapter 2The Treaty of Versailles
Chapter 2

The Treaty of Versailles

Germany was handed the treaty and told to sign it. It did so on June 28, 1919, in the Hall of Mirrors at Versailles, five years to the day after Sarajevo. The terms were severe. Germany returned Alsace and Lorraine to France and gave land to Poland, which gave Poland a corridor to the sea. Germany lost all its colonies. The coal-rich Saar was placed under League administration for fifteen years, Danzig became a free city, and Austria was forbidden to unite with Germany. Its army was limited to 100,000 men, with no tanks, no military aircraft, and a small navy, and the Rhineland was to remain free of German troops. Article 231, the so-called war guilt clause, said Germany and its allies were responsible for the war and its damage. On that basis, Germany owed reparations, which a commission set in 1921 at 132 billion gold marks, a huge sum.

The signing came after weeks of threat. Germany's new republican government had not wanted to sign, and the head of the government resigned rather than do it. The Allies warned that their armies would march again, and Germany's generals told the government that resistance would be hopeless. A week earlier German sailors held at Scapa Flow, in Scotland, had sunk their own fleet, seventy-four ships, rather than see it divided among the victors. The Hall of Mirrors was also the room where the German Empire had been proclaimed in January 1871, after the defeat of France. Both sides knew it.

Germans called the treaty a Diktat, a dictated peace, and almost all of them resented it. The treaty seemed too harsh to Germans, yet the French thought it too weak. Marshal Foch is said to have remarked that this was no peace, but an armistice for twenty years. Think about the dilemma. Germany had not been invaded and its factories were whole, so it remained the strongest nation in Europe by population and industry. The treaty humiliated it without taking from it the power to try again.

The treaty had critics among the victors too. John Maynard Keynes, a young British economist who had advised his government at the conference, resigned in despair and wrote a book arguing that a ruined Germany would drag all of Europe down with it. On the western bank of the Rhine, Allied troops were to stay for as long as fifteen years, a guarantee that France valued and Germans resented. And the sum the Germans owed was a figure on paper: how much they would pay, and how, would be argued over for the next decade.

Part 3

A New Map

Chapter 3A New Map
Chapter 3

A New Map

Other treaties dealt with Germany's allies. The empire of Austria-Hungary fell apart, and in its place stood Austria, Hungary, Czechoslovakia, and Yugoslavia, with parts going to Poland and Romania. Poland came back onto the map, and Finland, Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania were born from the old Russian lands. The principle of self-determination was applied unevenly. About three million Germans found themselves in Czechoslovakia, and Hungary lost two-thirds of its land. Millions of people were left as minorities in states ruled by a different nation. These grievances would return.

The new borders made as many problems as they solved. To give Poland its corridor to the sea, the treaty cut off East Prussia from the rest of Germany, and the port of Danzig, mostly German in population, was neither German nor Polish. Yugoslavia was a kingdom of Serbs, Croats, and Slovenes, led by Serbia, the little state whose quarrel with Austria had started the war. Czechoslovakia was the most prosperous and best governed of the new states, yet its German, Slovak, and Hungarian minorities did not all think of it as theirs. The treaty with Hungary, signed in 1920 at Trianon, left millions of Hungarians outside the country's new borders.

The Ottoman Empire was dismembered, too. A Turkish army under Mustafa Kemal, later called Atatürk, threw off the harsh peace imposed on Turkey and, in 1923, won a fairer treaty and a new republic. The Arab lands of the old empire were handled differently. The League of Nations gave them to Britain and France as mandates, to be governed until the peoples were ready to rule themselves. Britain took Iraq, Transjordan, and Palestine, and France took Syria and Lebanon. Some Arab leaders, who had been promised more during the war, were bitterly disappointed.

The promises of the war explain much of that disappointment. In 1915 a British official had written to Hussein, the ruler of Mecca, in terms the Arabs took as a pledge of an independent Arab state if they rose against the Turks. In 1916 Britain and France had secretly agreed to divide the region between them. In 1917 the British government declared its support for a national home for the Jewish people in Palestine. Those three promises could not all be kept. Hussein's son Faisal was proclaimed king of Syria in 1920, but French troops drove him out within months. Britain then made him king of Iraq, and his brother Abdullah ruled Transjordan under British oversight.

The Turkish story took a harder road than the quick summary suggests. The first treaty, signed at Sèvres in 1920 by the sultan's government, left the Turks only a part of Anatolia, and Greek troops had landed at Smyrna in 1919. Mustafa Kemal, an officer who had made his name at Gallipoli, rallied a new government at Ankara and drove the Greek army back to the sea in 1922. The sultanate was ended that year. The new treaty came in 1923 at Lausanne, together with an exchange of populations that moved well over a million people between Greece and Turkey.

Part 4

A League Without Teeth

Chapter 4A League Without Teeth
Chapter 4

A League Without Teeth

Wilson held the League of Nations to be the heart of the treaty. But the United States Senate refused to approve it. Senator Henry Cabot Lodge and others feared the League might commit America to wars it had not chosen. Wilson toured the country to rally support and suffered a stroke in October 1919. The Senate rejected the treaty in 1920. Germany would join in 1926, and the Soviet Union in 1934, but Italy and Japan would later walk out. Without America, and with Germany and Russia outside it at the start, the League had no army and no power to force its decisions. Britain and France were weakened by the war and unwilling to enforce the peace alone.

The League's weakness was built into its rules. Each of its main bodies, the Assembly and the Council, needed the agreement of all members to act, so any great power could block a decision. Its most powerful tool was a promise from members to defend one another's borders, in a clause called Article 10, and that was the clause Lodge and his allies most feared. It could ask members to cut off trade with an aggressor, but it had no army of its own. In small disputes, such as a quarrel between Finland and Sweden over the Aland Islands in 1921, it helped. Whether it could stop a great power that was willing to defy it had yet to be tested.

Part 5

Lenin's Russia

Chapter 5Lenin's Russia
Chapter 5

Lenin's Russia

While Paris argued, Russia was in flames. Last week you saw the Bolsheviks seize power in November 1917. Vladimir Lenin was a patient, ruthless organizer who believed a small, disciplined party should lead the working class. He argued that workers left alone would only seek better wages, and that a party of dedicated, professional revolutionaries had to guide them. The party took its authority from the councils of workers and soldiers, known as soviets. When elections in January 1918 gave the Bolsheviks only about a quarter of the seats in a new assembly, Lenin dissolved it. A secret police, the Cheka, soon hunted opponents. In July 1918 Bolshevik guards shot the former tsar, Nicholas II, and his family.

Lenin's habits of mind came from his own history. As a young man he saw his older brother hanged in 1887 for a plot against the tsar, and he spent years in prison, in Siberian exile, and abroad. In 1903 his followers, who won a vote at a party congress, took the name Bolsheviks, meaning the majority, though they did not remain one. After a woman shot and wounded Lenin in August 1918, the Cheka under Felix Dzerzhinsky began a campaign of terror, arresting and shooting thousands without trial.

A civil war between the Reds and the Whites, a mixed group of officers, liberals, and monarchists, lasted until 1921. The Whites were divided and had no common cause, while the Reds held the central cities and railways. Britain, France, the United States, and Japan sent troops at various times, but not enough to matter. Famine and the civil war killed millions. In 1921 sailors at Kronstadt, once heroes of the revolution, rose against the Bolsheviks, and the revolt was crushed. Lenin, shaken, retreated from the harshest policies and allowed small private trade under the New Economic Policy. In 1922 the Bolsheviks proclaimed the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics.

Two men did more than any others to win the war for the Reds. Leon Trotsky built the Red Army out of volunteers and conscripts, and he drafted thousands of former tsarist officers, placing political officers beside them to watch their loyalty. To feed the cities and the army, the Bolsheviks seized grain from the peasants, who responded by planting less and hiding what they grew. When drought struck in 1921, famine spread along the Volga. An American relief group led by Herbert Hoover fed millions of Russians. The New Economic Policy ended the seizures, and in their place peasants paid a fixed tax and could sell the rest. Lenin called it a retreat. The state still held the banks, the railways, and the biggest factories.

Recall that Marx expected revolution in the most industrial countries. It had come in a land of peasants, because war had broken the old government and a small, determined party was ready to seize the moment. Lenin died in January 1924. Who would succeed him, and what kind of state would he build? Those questions are the next lesson's story.
